Each variable forms a column.
In long format, all repeated measurements (like scores over time) are represented by a single “value” column (e.g., Score) and a single “key” column (e.g., Timepoint). This is tidy, whereas in wide format, the key variable’s values are incorrectly stored as column names (e.g., Score_T1, Score_T2).
Each observation forms a row.
In long format, a single row represents a single measurement, which is the smallest and most consistent unit of observation (e.g., “Participant P001’s score at Time 1”).

title: PSY6422 - Data Management & Visualisation
section: What is the Grammar of Graphics?
text:
What is the Grammar of Graphics?

A set of rules for building statistical plots layer by layer.
A plot is not a single object, but rather a combination of independent components:

Data: The dataset you’re using.
Aesthetic Mappings: How variables in your data are mapped to visual properties (e.g., x position, y position, color, size).
Geometric Objects: The shapes you use to represent the data (e.g., points, lines, bars).
Statistical Transformations: Calculations on the data (e.g., a histogram’s counts, a box plot’s quartiles).
Scales: The range of the axes and colours.
Coordinate System: The space the plot lives in (e.g., Cartesian, polar).
Facets: How you split the data into subplots based on a variable.

title: PSY6422 - Data Management & Visualisation
text:
The ggplot2 Template

Every ggplot2 plot follows this core structure:

ggplot(data = your_data_frame, mapping = aes(x = variable_x, y = variable_y)) + geom_type()

You’ll always start with ggplot() to define the data and the main aesthetic mappings.

ggplot() is like the blank canvas
aes() (short for “aesthetics”) is where you tell ggplot which variables go where
You then add layers using the + operator

title: PSY6422 - Data Management & Visualisation
text:
The + Operator

ggplot2 is built on layers. You add them one at a time using the + operator.


The base ggplot() call is the first layer
geom_*() functions are layers that add the visual representation (points, lines, bars)
labs() adds labels and titles
theme_*() changes the overall appearance


This layering approach is what makes ggplot2 so powerful and flexible.

ggplot2 Bar Plots - Counts vs. Summaries

A common point of confusion is when to use geom_bar() vs. geom_col().


geom_bar(): Use this when you want to plot the count of a categorical variable. It automatically performs the counting.
geom_col(): Use this when you have a pre-calculated summary statistic (like a mean or sum). It requires both an x and a y aesthetic.

title: PSY6422 - Data Management & Visualisation
section: ggplot2 Bar Plots - Counts vs. Summaries
text:
ggplot2 Bar Plots - Counts vs. Summaries

If we want to visualise the number of cars for each cylinder type (cyl), we would use geom_bar(). We would only need to provide the x aesthetic.


ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = as.factor(cyl))) +
  geom_bar(fill = "skyblue", color = "black") +
  labs(title = "Count of Cars by Cylinder Type", 
       x = "Cylinder Type", y = "Number of Cars")

ggplot2 Bar Plots - Counts vs. Summaries

If we want to visualise the average horsepower for each cylinder type (cyl), we would first calculate the mean and then pass both x and y aesthetics to geom_col()


# Calculating the average horsepower 
mtcars_summary <- mtcars %>%
group_by(cyl) %>%
summarise(avg_hp = mean(hp), .groups = "drop")



# Making the plot 
ggplot(mtcars_summary, aes(x = as.factor(cyl), y = avg_hp)) +
  geom_col(fill = "skyblue", color = "black") +
  labs(title = "Average Horsepower by Cylinder Type", 
       x = "Cylinder Type", y = "Mean Horsepower")

Faceting: Small Multiples

A strength of ggplot2 is its ability to create small multiples, or subplots, for different categories. This is called faceting.


facet_wrap() creates a series of plots that wrap to fill the space.
facet_grid() creates a grid of plots, allowing you to split by two variables.

title: PSY6422 - Data Management & Visualisation
text:
ggplot2 facet_wrap()

Suppose we want to produce a separate scatter plot for each cylinder type. We can specify facet_wrap(~cyl).


ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = hp, y = mpg)) +
  geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(~ cyl) +
  labs(title = "MPG vs. Horsepower, separated by Cylinders")

title: PSY6422 - Data Management & Visualisation
text:
A More Complex Plot

We start with ggplot(), the base layer of the plot. We specify our data (mtcars), our x-axis variable (hp), our y-axis variable (mpg), and we assign a different colour to each unique cylinder (cyl) count.


ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = hp, y = mpg, color = as.factor(cyl))) +

title: PSY6422 - Data Management & Visualisation
text:
A More Complex Plot

Next, we use geom_point() to tell ggplot2 we want a scatter plot. We can use alpha to set the transparency of the points (1 = fully opaque; 0 = fully transparent). We can change the size of the points (size) to make them bigger.


ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = hp, y = mpg, color = as.factor(cyl))) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7, size = 3) +

title: PSY6422 - Data Management & Visualisation
text:
A More Complex Plot

In our next layer, we add a smoothing line. geom_smooth() calculates and draws a line of best fit between x and y for each colour group (cyl). lm specifies that we are using a linear model. Because color is mapped to cyl, ggplot2 will draw a separate line for each cylinder type.
se = FALSE removes the standard error (shaded gray confidence interval) around the smoothing line.
linetype = "dotted" changes the style of the line from solid to dotted.


ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = hp, y = mpg, color = as.factor(cyl))) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7, size = 3) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, linetype = "dotted") +

title: PSY6422 - Data Management & Visualisation
text:
A More Complex Plot

Next, we add a labelling layer using labs() to customise the plot’s labels.
By specifying color = "Cylinders", ggplot2 sets the title of the legend that was created automatically by mapping cyl to color in the aes() function.


ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = hp, y = mpg, color = as.factor(cyl))) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7, size = 3) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, linetype = "dotted") +
  labs(title = "MPG vs. Horsepower by Cylinder Type",
       x = "Horsepower", y = "Miles Per Gallon",
       color = "Cylinders") +

text:
A More Complex Plot

In our final layer, we specify the theme using the pre-built black and white theme, theme_bw()


ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = hp, y = mpg, color = as.factor(cyl))) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7, size = 3) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, linetype = "dotted") +
  labs(title = "MPG vs. Horsepower by Cylinder Type",
       x = "Horsepower", y = "Miles Per Gallon",
       color = "Cylinders") +
  theme_bw()

title: PSY6422 - Data Management & Visualisation
text:
The Power of the Pipe!
What is the pipe?

The pipe operator written as |> or %>%, takes an ouput of one function and ‘pipes’ it to the next function
It is like a conveyor belt, each function performing an action on the data before passing it on to the next step
The pipe is where the tidyverse comes into its own - helping us to build clear, step-by-step workflows


Shortcut! Ctrl + Shift + M on Windows and Cmd + Shift + M on a Mac

title: PSY6422 - Data Management & Visualisation
text:
The Pipe in Action
Without the pipe, we typically have to nest functions

# From a dataset, select participants aged over 25 
# and show the first few rows
head(filter(my_data, age > 25))

 The pipe makes the code much more intuitive and readable

# From a dataset, select participants aged over 25 
# and show the first few rows
data %>% 
  filter(my_data > 25) %>% 
  head()

title: PSY6422 - Data Management & Visualisation
text:
The Pipe in Action
The value of the pipe becomes clear when we start adding steps to the transformations we execute on our dataset

# A simple pipeline
my_data %>% 
  filter(Condition == "Treatment") %>% # Step 1: Keep only 'Treatment' group
  select(ID, Q1, Q2) %>% # Step 2: Select ID and two questionnaire scores
  mutate(total_score = Q1 + Q2) # Step 3: Create a new variable 'total_score'

title: PSY6422 - Data Management & Visualisation
text:
group_by()
Often we will want to perform an operation on only a group of our participants

e.g. by experimental condition or participant group


The group_by() function tells R how to split your data into these logical groups.

# Group the dataset by the 'Condition' variable
df %>%
  group_by(Condition)


This function doesn’t change the visible output much on its own, but it’s a critical first step. It adds grouping information to the tibble, so that any subsequent functions will operate on each group separately.

title: PSY6422 - Data Management & Visualisation
text:
group_by() and summarise()
We can use group_by() with summarise() to calculate summary statistics by group

# Group by Condition, then calculate the mean age for each group
df %>%
  group_by(Condition) %>%
  summarise(mean_q1 = mean(Q1), n = n())

# A tibble: 2 × 3
  Condition mean_q1     n
  <chr>       <dbl> <int>
1 Control      4.33     6
2 Treatment   NA        4



Here, we’re creating a new tibble with one row for each group (Condition). We’ve created two new variables in our output: mean_age, which holds the average age for each group, and n, which counts the number of observations in each group using the n() function.

ifelse() is useful here!


# Create a new group column based on whether participants responded 
# over a value on a questionnaire item
my_data %>%
  mutate(group = ifelse(Q1 > 3, "A", "B")) 

# A tibble: 5 × 6
  ID      age Condition    Q1    Q2 group
  <chr> <dbl> <chr>     <dbl> <dbl> <chr>
1 P001     30 Control       4     5 A    
2 P002     22 Treatment     5     4 A    
3 P003     45 Control       5     5 A    
4 P004     19 Treatment     3     4 B    
5 P005     28 Control       2     3 B    



In this example, we’re using ifelse() inside of mutate(). The ifelse() function takes three arguments: a condition (age > 25), a value if the condition is true (“Older”), and a value if the condition is false (“Younger”). This is a powerful way to recode your data for analysis.

Changing Data Types with mutate()
As we learned last week, data type is very important. We can use mutate() with as. functions to change data type

as.numeric(): Converts data into a numeric type (for continuous numbers).
as.character(): Converts data into a character type (for text).
as.factor(): Converts data into a factor (for categorical data with defined levels).

Changing Data Types with mutate()
Use glimpse() to inspect the data types

What’s wrong here?


glimpse(bad_type_data)

Rows: 3
Columns: 3
$ ID        <chr> "P001", "P002", "P003"
$ age       <chr> "30", "22", "45"
$ Condition <chr> "Control", "Treatment", "Control"

title: PSY6422 - Data Management & Visualisation
text:
Changing Data Types with mutate()
Correct the data type using mutate() and as.numeric()

corrected_data <- bad_type_data %>%
  mutate(age = as.numeric(age))
# Check the new data types
glimpse(corrected_data)

Rows: 3
Columns: 3
$ ID        <chr> "P001", "P002", "P003"
$ age       <dbl> 30, 22, 45
$ Condition <chr> "Control", "Treatment", "Control"



In this code, we take our bad_type_data, and pipe it into mutate(). We’re creating a new age column by applying as.numeric() to the old age column. When we check the result, we see that age is now a <dbl> or “double,” which is a numeric type, and we can perform calculations on it. This is a very common and useful step in data wrangling.

Wide and Long Format
Last week we introduced the concept of long and wide data formats. 
tidyverse provides two key functions for converting between them:

pivot_longer(): converts wide data to long
Takes multiple columns and collapses them into two columns: one for the variable names and one for the values.
Example: Turn Q1, Q2, Q3 columns into one ‘Question’ column and one ‘Score’ column.

text:
pivot_longer()

#Data in wide format
head(my_data)

3 P003     45 Control       5     5
4 P004     19 Treatment     3     4
5 P005     28 Control       2     3

text:
pivot_longer()

my_data_long <- my_data %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(Q1, Q2), # Columns to be collapsed
    names_to = "Question", # Name of new column that holds old column names
    values_to = "Score" # Name of new column that holds the values
  )
